milestones.title: Panyu founded by the Qin
milestones.detail: Panyu was established on the Pearl River as the seat of Nanhai Commandery during the Qin conquest of the Baiyue lands.

milestones.title: Capital of the Nanyue kingdom
milestones.detail: After the fall of the Qin, General Zhao Tuo founded the kingdom of Nanyue and made Panyu its capital.
milestones.source: Taylor (1983), The Birth of Vietnam, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#History

milestones.title: Han conquest of Nanyue
milestones.detail: Han armies under Lu Bode and Yang Pu took Panyu and annexed Nanyue; the city became a Han provincial capital.
milestones.source: Morton & Lewis, China: Its History and Culture, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#History

milestones.title: Seat of Guang Prefecture
milestones.detail: Panyu became the seat of the new Guang Prefecture (Guangzhou), which gave the city its modern name.

milestones.title: Port sacked by Arab and Persian raiders
milestones.detail: With China distracted by the An Lushan Rebellion, Arab and Persian pirates sacked the city on 30 October 758.

milestones.title: Capital of the Southern Han
milestones.detail: Liu Yan made the city the capital of his 'Great Yue' or Southern Han state, which lasted from 917 to 971.

milestones.title: Qing siege and massacre
milestones.detail: On 24 November 1650 Shang Kexi's forces took the city after a prolonged siege and killed up to 70,000 people.

milestones.title: Canton System: China's only port for Western trade
milestones.detail: From 1757 to 1842 the Thirteen Factories on the riverfront were the only legal place for foreign trade with China.
milestones.source: Chatwin, Jonathan, The Southern Tour, p. xviii, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#History

milestones.title: British capture Canton in the First Opium War
milestones.detail: British forces captured the city on 18 March 1841; the 1842 treaty ended its trade monopoly as other treaty ports opened.

milestones.title: Arrow War: factories burned, city occupied
milestones.detail: The foreign factories were destroyed in 1856 and British and French forces occupied the city until 1861; Shamian Island was divided into British and French concessions in 1859.
milestones.source: Webster's Geographical Dictionary (1960) and Farris (2007), via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Guangzhou

milestones.title: Kowloon-Canton Railway; Second Guangzhou Uprising
milestones.detail: The railway to Kowloon began operating, and an uprising in the city that year was a forerunner of the 1911 Revolution.

milestones.title: City walls demolished
milestones.detail: Work began in June 1919 on demolishing the city wall to make way for wider streets and tramways; it took three years.
milestones.source: Lee, Edward Bing-Shuey (1936), Modern Canton, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#Transportation

milestones.title: Japanese occupation
milestones.detail: Japanese forces occupied the city from 21 October 1938 until 16 September 1945.

milestones.title: People's Liberation Army enters Guangzhou
milestones.detail: The city, briefly the seat of the Nationalist government, was captured on 14 October 1949; retreating forces blew up the Haizhu Bridge.

milestones.title: Guangzhou Metro opens
milestones.detail: The first metro line opened in 1997, making Guangzhou the fourth mainland Chinese city with an underground railway.

milestones.title: Asian Games and Canton Tower
milestones.detail: Guangzhou hosted the 2010 Asian Games in November; the Canton Tower and the International Finance Center were completed the same year.

landmarks.name: Huaisheng Mosque minaret (Guangta)
landmarks.note: Date disputed: traditionally about 627 (Tang, Zhenguan era); other scholars date the minaret to the later Tang or the Song dynasty.

landmarks.name: Flower Pagoda, Temple of the Six Banyan Trees
landmarks.source: https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/六榕寺 (height 57.6 m with finial) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Six_Banyan_Trees ; position from OpenStreetMap (WGS-84)
landmarks.note: Built 1097; rebuilt 1373 after a fire and restored in 1900.

landmarks.name: Baiyun Hotel
landmarks.note: 93.5 m to roof; 117 m with antenna.

landmarks.name: Canton Tower
landmarks.source: CTBUH Skyscraper Center, https://www.skyscrapercenter.com/building/canton-tower/9385 ; position from OpenStreetMap (WGS-84)

notes: Start date: the Qin foundation of Panyu in 214 BC as seat of Nanhai Commandery is the standard documented date and is the date used by the sources consulted. The historic core point is the Nanyue Kingdom Palace Museum on Zhongshan 4th Road, located via OpenStreetMap. Older tradition speaks of a settlement called Nanwucheng (said to exist by 1100 BC, or founded under King Nan of Zhou, 314-256 BC); this is treated as legend and not used. Population: nothing was found before AD 700. The 700 and 800 points are Modelski's (200,000) and the series from 1000 to 1925 is Chandler's, both as digitised by Reba et al. (2016); the two series do not join smoothly (Chandler has 40,000 for 1000). All are scholarly estimates for the walled city and suburbs, not counts. The 1936 figure is an estimate from Webster's Geographical Dictionary. Another estimate of 400,000 for 1879 (Lo et al. 1977, via Wikipedia's timeline) conflicts with Chandler's 670,000 for 1875 and was left out. No census figure before 1950 was found. Landmarks: skyscrapers and the Canton Tower are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center; older structures take heights from Wikipedia (English or Chinese) and positions from OpenStreetMap. The Huaisheng minaret's date is disputed and Pazhou Pagoda's height is approximate; both are marked 'estimated'. The cathedral's tower height is as given on Wikipedia (52.76 m); other figures circulate. Left out: Guangzhou Hotel (1968), whose CTBUH height (104 m) conflicts with other accounts; Haizhu Bridge, Chen Clan Ancestral Hall and Guangxiao Temple (no sourced height).
